title: Our Practice Affects Others
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley describes a stubborn resistance to practice and the question "Where is the joy?", which Michael Newton offered in a practice discussion at Samish. Seishu recalls Thanissaro Bhikkhu's advice that the mind is like a committee, and Norman Fischer's counsel to make a best effort and let the worry go. Seishu then reads a letter from daughter Gillian in New Orleans, who passed the question along to friends, including a note left on a sun visor before a road trip to Montana. The letter shows practice reaching people in ways no one plans. Seishu closes by comparing the return to "Where's the joy?" with returning to the breath.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.

I am going to talk about how our practice affects other people tonight, and how it can affect other people in our lives, how it moves around from person to person, sometimes having a reach that is surprising and unpredictable.
I will use an example from my practice.
Those of you who know me, and I have talked about this before, know that I struggle with some things about practice.
I think most of us have some things that make practice difficult at times, sometimes family obligations, physical limitations, doubts about practice, trouble making the time for it, things like that.
In my case, the resistance is a little hard to describe.
Some of you have heard this before.
I just call it resistance to practice.
The way it looks is before a weekend or a week-long sesshin, I might start to feel a little down, like I am going to miss the things I would be doing if I was home.
I am going to miss my wife Carolyn.
Maybe I have some worries: what if I don't sleep well?
What if my knees hurt?
Maybe some upset about how much time and energy practice takes.
That is what it tends to look like; it could be any of those things, usually, thankfully, not all of them at once.
At the same time, I have always felt that it has been worth the time and effort and all the other sacrifices I have had to make.
I get a great deal out of this meditation practice both at home and practicing with the sangha.
I have really felt that over the years.
I tend to ignore my resistance; I just participate in most of the things that we do.
But the resistance surprises me.
I thought after this many years of practice, it would either be gone or it would be pretty small.
It has changed a little bit, but not very much, unfortunately.
I hear people say, "I am really looking forward to this sesshin, whether it is a weekend or a week long.
I can't wait."
I don't feel that way.
The other thing I do is look at Tim or Chris or Nancy here at Red Cedar or Michael and Kate at Mountain Rain and Ruth and Rick.
It seems to me that they have more joy in their practice than I do.
I have wondered, what is wrong with me?
I don't have more enthusiasm, more joy.
What is wrong with me that I don't feel that way?
I compare myself to what I think they experience, and I feel like I am missing something.
Of course, I realize that what I think someone else experiences is often very different than what they actually do experience.
But still, I do these comparisons, and it just seems like other people have a little more fun and more enjoyment than I do.
I feel like I come up short in some ways.
I have talked with Norman Fischer, my teacher.
I have talked with Tim.
I have talked with lots of people about this resistance.
That has been helpful, but it is still around.
I was just remembering that Thanissaro Bhikkhu is a teacher in the Thai forest tradition.
He is coming here in the middle of September; he is down in California.
He is a wonderful teacher, and I have seen him here a couple of different times.
I remember explaining this to him, my bad attitude.
I wish I didn't have it.
What should I do?
He had some very helpful advice.
He said, "Your mind is like a committee.
You are going to have a lot of opinions and you just have to be careful which ones you listen to."
That was helpful.
I have my resistance; I can hear it, but I don't have to listen to it.
I don't have to act on it.
A couple of years ago, I think it was Samish 2008.
I had a practice discussion about this with Michael Newton.
Michael, if any of you don't know him, he is a priest up in Canada in the Mountain Rain Zen community.
This was the topic: my resistance, how others seem to have more joy in their practice, and why isn't there more joy in my practice.
Some of you may not know Michael.
He was ordained six or seven years ago, Tim, something like that.
He lived in Japan for a number of years when he was younger and practiced there.
He has been a long-time student of Norman Fischer's, like many of us have been.
Michael and I had our talk.
He suggested that I really study this in a couple of ways: with the resistance, ask what is this, to study it deeply like a koan, and also to ask the question, "Where is the joy?"
He said, "You can ask the sky, you can ask the grass, you can ask the rocks, you can ask the trees, you can ask the birds, where is the joy?"
I really liked that.
He also suggested that I offer some things as part of my practice, like giving talks or classes, things that would challenge me and stretch me a little bit.
I was pleased with our talk, and I looked forward to doing the things he suggested.
I spent some time asking, "What is this?" and "Where is the joy?"
What is this when resistance arises, and where is the joy when I was feeling the struggles of practice?
Really trying to make some space to pay attention for a while, not to be so busy but just to ask the question and just stop.
As you probably know, finding an answer, it's not like joy is located somewhere.
Finding an answer to these questions isn't the point, but keeping the question in mind over and over again, over time, that's the practice.
Just asking the questions has been transformative.
Looking at the sky or the trees or the clouds or the grass and asking the question is completely different than being caught up in some unhappiness.
When I ask the clouds or the trees or the grass, "Where is the joy?"
I really look at them, and I notice how beautiful they are.

That's a wonderful thing to be aware of even when you're in the middle of some difficulty, regardless of what's going on right now in my life, just to be aware of some of the beautiful things around us.
When I really look at resistance by asking, "What is this?" then I take the time to really look at it.
Much of my resistance is just worry about what might happen.
Usually, the things I worry about don't happen, and if they do, they cause pretty small problems.
For example, for me, I think one of the hardest things about meditation is when I'm sleepy.
I really don't like that at all.
I hate sitting in the zendo, almost nodding off, fighting to wake up.
I'd rather have physical pain because I'm awake when I have physical pain.
I have some things I can do to work with pain that are actually pretty effective.
Nancy, you probably disagree with me on this.
You might prefer sleeping.
I feel at the mercy of sleepiness; there's just nothing I can do about it.
I just have to wait it out.
I might worry about, at a residential session, "What if I don't sleep well?
Then I'll have a difficult day."
I've been to many residential sessions, and sometimes I don't sleep well.
Usually once or twice in a week I don't sleep well.
Actually, it's not too bad.
I've learned when I can't sleep to just lay quietly and meditate and relax.
Even if I don't get many hours of sleep, I often feel pretty rested.
The sleepiness isn't too big a deal.
I get through the day pretty well.
I've also learned not to tell myself, "Oh my god, it's two o'clock in the morning.
I'm screwed.
Tomorrow is going to be ruined."
I don't do that.
I just keep relaxing, and I tell myself, "I'll probably be okay.
I'll probably get through the day okay."
I'm grateful that I sleep well most of the time and that I don't get caught up very much in my worry about not sleeping.
Another part of my resistance is worrying about making mistakes.
When I make mistakes, I get upset at myself, and then I worry that others might be disappointed or upset.
For example, when I've been in Jisha, the teacher's attendant, at a crowded retreat, I might worry, "Is everybody going to get a chance to have an interview with Norman?
What if there's not enough time?"
If there's not enough time, I have to pick who sees him and who doesn't.
I don't like being in that position.

I've talked to Norman about this, and he has said, and this is another bit of good advice, that in these kinds of situations, you make your best effort, you accept the help of other people, and then whatever happens, happens, and you accept that too.
That's kind of like having faith that life unfolds the way it ought to if you're making your best effort.
He said the worry is extra and it just makes for more suffering for you.
There's no point in it.

I've realized through practice how important it is not to let this kind of worry stop me from extending myself or trying new things, to take risks and sometimes to fail, to bear the pain of a failure with compassion for myself and compassion for other people who are also making mistakes.
It's not that bad.
I don't like making mistakes, but when I look back on it, I've got ten fingers and toes.
Life's been okay even with the mistakes I've made.
If I let my fear of making mistakes have too much power, then my life becomes so much more limited and restricted.
These are some of the examples of the struggles I've had with practice and some of the talks I've had.
When I'm curious about my resistance without judgment, just looking at it, not only can I understand it at a deeper level, but I also notice a real change in my body.
I feel an openness in my body and my breathing; there's really no tension.
When I'm stewing about it and being critical, like, "Why is this still here?
I wish I could get rid of this," there really is physical tension.
I can feel it in my stomach.
I can feel it in my jaw.
My breathing is restricted.
So the talk with Michael was very helpful to be curious and to ask, "What is this?" and really study it.
You might be wondering, what does this have to do with my topic about how our practice affects other people?
I'm getting to that.
I have a daughter, Gillian, and she's thirty now.
She's had some experience with meditation.
When she was fifteen, our whole family, my wife and Gillian and I, came to our first weekend session with the Bellingham Zen practice group and Norman Fischer.
Bellingham Zen, of course, morphed into Red Cedar.
So Gillian did that.
She also spent a month at the Great Vow Zen Monastery when she was in college.
And then she does some meditation practice now.
But she lives in New Orleans, so she's a long ways away, and I only see her a couple of times a year.
We talk on the phone maybe two or three times a month.
But neither one of us are phone people.
I don't like talking on the phone much, even with people I love.
I mean, I can do it maybe twenty minutes, but I just don't like being on the phone.
So a couple of years ago, we started writing letters to each other, and that is a wonderful thing to do.
I highly recommend it.
It's so much better than email, even though it's slower.
There's just something about using pen and paper and putting it down in your own words and writing it that leads to much deeper communication.
I know that I'm much more thoughtful about what I say when I'm writing than when I'm talking.
And I often write things that I might never get to when I'm talking.
And then reading a letter that's been written in somebody else's hand, holding the paper, reading their words, it's so personal.
And then looking at it again, thinking about it, thinking about what's been written, it just stirs up a much deeper response.
So this has been a really wonderful thing we've been doing the last couple years, maybe the last five or six years.
So I put something in a letter to Gillian about this talk I had with Michael and my resistance and "Where's the joy?"
I can't even remember what I wrote.
And then a couple months later, I got a letter back from her.
And I think I'll just read you the section of the letter that applies to this.
First of all, the weather has been perfect.
It's warm with a healthy warm breeze that ruffles leaves, feathers, hair, and garbage.
I went to meditation across the street this morning, and on my walk back home, I felt like I was seeing the beauty in everything for the first time in a while.
All the banana trees, the colorful houses, everything so green and lush.
Yesterday, I told my friend John, the one who has the same birthday as you, Dad, about "Where's the joy?"
I don't know if I mentioned this before, but when you told me about it, just asking oneself that question throughout the day, I started doing that.
And I started looking for the joy even in a really miserable time.
It was such a good thing to come back to over and over again.
I told Daniel about it, even stuck a note that said, "Where's the joy?" on his sun visor before he left on the road trip to Montana so he would discover it.
He told me that he moved it to the steering wheel when he found it.
He said that question was sort of the point of the trip itself.
So I told John about it.
When I saw him today at meditation, he said that he'd been thinking about that question ever since.
He said it had really profoundly affected him.
It was, in fact, sort of an answer to a question that he'd had on his mind for a while.
We talked about the profundity of the word joy, how it feels like it rises up from inside instead of being this stuck on exterior feeling the way I think about happiness.
I wanted to tell you about how meaningful that question has been to several of us who've been having a hard time of it down here in New Orleans.
So when I read that, I was really surprised and moved.
I had no idea and no expectation that there would be any kind of an impact.
I often talk to Gillian, and she talks to me about her practice and things like that.
That by itself is a good reason to practice, just to be able to have a positive impact on other people.
But of course, it would be a trap to have that expectation, to think, "Well, I'm going to practice so that I can help other people."
Michael's advice to me was very helpful.
I mentioned it to Gillian, and I passed it on to her friends.
You can just see how something like that can have a much wider impact than one could ever imagine.
Her letter kind of re-inspired me to work on the question more consistently and deeply.
When I re-read it, it has that same effect.
To keep it up, it's like a loop.
I think this is what we do here.
We support and inspire each other.
All of us here who sit together can come up with examples like this.
I certainly feel supported and encouraged in my practice every time I show up here.
Wednesday night is the foundation of my practice.
And on the weeks when I don't come to Wednesday night meditation, I can feel it.
I can just feel the difference, the momentum of practice, the daily meditation, the attention day-to-day to how we're living off the cushion.
That's diminished a little bit.
So I really feel like we support each other just by showing up.
Most of the time I don't think we hear much about how practice can have a positive impact on other people, or maybe that's just me.
I tend to pay more attention to the problems that I cause others by being impatient or forgetful or stingy, the things I need to keep working on.
But I think it's really nice once in a while to just be reminded of the ways in which practice is very helpful.

And I still have a lot of work to do on my resistance: accepting it rather than wanting it to go away, being curious about it, "What is this?" instead of feeling judgmental about its existence or feeling like I'm less than because I have it.
And continuing to ask, "Where's the joy?" especially when I'm stewing about something.
And writing this has reminded me that it's pretty easy to forget these things and just let the day-to-day details of life take over.
It's hard to pay attention to things like this month after month in the midst of a life with work and family and all the other things that occupy our time and attention.
And, of course, established habits of thinking are more than happy to return if I'm not vigilant.
And it's just like returning to the breath over and over and over again when the mind wanders during meditation, returning to patience, curiosity, and non-judgmental questioning.
So this is what I want to talk to you about tonight.
And thank you for listening.
